title: Design a Bounded Blocking Queue
summary: Thirty lines of code and an hour of conversation. This is the question that finds out whether you actually understand condition variables, or have only ever copied the pattern — and the lost-wakeup bug is where it finds out.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Whether you know why the wait is a **`while`** and not an **`if`**. Everything else in this problem — the deque, the capacity check, the size method — is trivial. That one keyword is the question, and the interviewer will ask you to justify it.
The problem
Implement a thread-safe FIFO queue with a fixed capacity:

items: `enqueue(int element)` — adds to the tail. **Blocks** while the queue is full.
`int dequeue()` — removes from the head and returns it. **Blocks** while the queue is empty.

blocks.text: Multiple producer and consumer threads call these concurrently. No busy-waiting, no dropped elements, no deadlock.
Clarify before you code

items.title: Is a timeout or a non-blocking variant needed?
items.text: `offer(e, timeout)` and `poll(timeout)` are the real-world API. Confirm scope — the timed version has its own trap, covered below.

items.title: Does the queue ever shut down?
items.text: A queue nobody can close means consumers block forever at the end of the run. Real systems need a poison pill or a `close()`; LeetCode does not.

items.title: Strict FIFO across producers?
items.text: Yes within the queue. Note that *which* blocked producer wakes first is not FIFO unless the lock is fair — and fairness costs throughput.

items.title: Can I use the standard library?
items.text: `ArrayBlockingQueue` is exactly this. Ask, because if the answer is yes the interview is over in one line — which itself tells you the answer is no.

blocks.text: The structure

blocks.title: One lock, two waiting rooms
blocks.caption: Separate conditions for *not full* and *not empty* mean a producer finishing wakes a **consumer**, not another producer. One shared condition works but wakes the wrong threads constantly.

blocks.text: The code
Why `while` and not `if`

blocks.title: Three independent reasons, and you should be able to give all three
blocks.text: **1. Spurious wakeups.** `await()` is permitted by the JLS to return without any signal at all. **2. Barging.** Between the signal and the woken thread reacquiring the lock, a *third* thread can enter, take the lock and take the slot — the condition was true when signalled and false by the time you run. **3. `signalAll`.** If several waiters wake for one slot, only one can have it. In all three cases the woken thread must **re-check**, and `if` does not re-check.
`signal` or `signalAll`

blocks.caption: Both are correct here. Knowing why is the follow-up.
rows: Thundering herd — everyone wakes, one wins, the rest re-block
Yes — a producer only ever signals consumers
**No** — may wake a producer when a consumer was needed
Waiters want different conditions, or the state change unblocks several

blocks.title: The sentence that lands
blocks.text: *“Two conditions let me use `signal` instead of `signalAll`, because a producer only ever needs to wake a consumer. With a single shared condition I would be forced into `signalAll` to avoid waking the wrong kind of thread and deadlocking.”*
The `synchronized` version
If the interviewer bans `ReentrantLock`, the monitor version is the same shape with one real loss.

blocks.title: `notify()` here is a deadlock
blocks.text: An object monitor has exactly **one** wait set, so producers and consumers queue together. `notify()` picks an arbitrary waiter — if a producer wakes another producer while the queue is still full, both go back to waiting and the system stalls with work available. `notifyAll()` is mandatory in the monitor version, and that is precisely the cost that two `Condition` objects buy you out of.
The semaphore version

blocks.filename: Semaphores — no explicit waiting at all

blocks.title: Elegant, and be ready for the trap
blocks.text: The counting semaphores *are* the capacity invariant, so there is no condition to re-check and no `while`. Note the ordering: acquire the semaphore **before** the mutex. Reverse them and a thread holding the mutex blocks on a semaphore that only a mutex-holder can release — a textbook deadlock, and a favourite thing to ask about.
Complexity

rows: O(1) once the lock is held
One lock; every operation serialises. See below

blocks.title: One lock is a throughput ceiling
blocks.text: Producers and consumers touch opposite ends of the queue but contend on the same lock. `LinkedBlockingQueue` uses **two** locks — one per end — so a producer and a consumer can run genuinely in parallel. Naming that is a strong senior signal; implementing it is usually out of scope.
Follow-ups you should have ready

items.title: Add a timeout
items.text: `notFull.awaitNanos(remaining)` in the loop. The trap: on a spurious wake you must recompute the *remaining* time, not restart the full timeout — otherwise a 1-second offer can block for minutes.

items.title: Add a non-blocking `offer` / `poll`
items.text: `tryLock`, check, return false rather than waiting. Now the queue supports back-pressure without blocking a caller.

items.title: Shut the queue down
items.text: A `closed` flag checked inside the wait loop, plus `signalAll` so every waiter re-checks and exits. Without it, consumers block forever at end of stream.

items.title: Add a dead letter queue
items.text: Listed as the follow-up on the reported OpenAI question. Failed items go to a second bounded queue — and it must be bounded too, or a poison message becomes an OOM.

items.title: Make it lock-free
items.text: A Michael-Scott queue for the unbounded case; bounded needs a ring buffer with CAS on head and tail. Say the words, and say it is rarely worth it against `ArrayBlockingQueue`.

items.title: Multiple priorities
items.text: A heap instead of a deque, and FIFO within a priority needs a sequence number as the tiebreaker or equal-priority items reorder.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: `capacity = 1` — degenerates to a handoff; every enqueue blocks until the previous is consumed.
`capacity = 0` — either reject at construction, or implement a synchronous handoff. Do not silently accept and deadlock.
`InterruptedException` must propagate, not be swallowed. Catching and ignoring it makes the thread uncancellable.
`unlock()` in a `finally` — an exception between lock and unlock wedges every other thread permanently.
`size()` is a snapshot and is stale the moment it returns. Say so; do not let a caller use it to decide whether to enqueue.
Interrupt while waiting → the thread must leave the wait loop without consuming an element.

blocks.text: What you are graded on

rows: Two, and explains the `signal` versus `signalAll` consequence
`notifyAll()`, and explains the single wait set
Semaphore before mutex, and names the deadlock

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–4** clarify timeouts, shutdown, library use. **4–8** draw one lock and two conditions. **8–18** write it — it is thirty lines. **18–26** explain `while` with the three-thread timeline; this is the part they are grading. **26–34** `signal` versus `signalAll`, and the monitor version. **34–45** timeouts or the dead letter queue.
